---
title: "Lecture: AR, MA, ACF/PACF and ARIMA (slides 80 to 125)"
---

Today's lecture covered slides 80 to 125. We started with AR and MA models on their own, then moved on to how to pick between them using the ACF and PACF, and finished with how they combine into ARIMA.

**What AR and MA are built on.** The main difference between the two is what each model is built on. An AR(p) model is built on lagged values of the series itself, whereas an MA(q) model is built on lagged errors. Before this lecture I saw both as just "using the past", without separating that one uses the actual observed values and the other uses the shocks the model could not explain.

**Picking the model with the ACF and PACF.** We then looked at how to use the ACF and PACF plots to decide which model fits. The slides summarise this in a table:

| Process | ACF | PACF |
|---|---|---|
| White noise | No significant spikes | No significant spikes |
| AR(p) | Decays gradually | Cuts off after lag p |
| MA(q) | Cuts off after lag q | Decays gradually |
| ARMA(p, q) | Decays gradually | Decays gradually |

For an AR(1), $y_t$ only depends directly on $y_{t-1}$. The PACF removes the indirect correlation that passes through the lags in between, so it cuts off after lag 1. The ACF still decays slowly, because $y_t$ is linked to $y_{t-2}$ and $y_{t-3}$ through that chain. MA is the other way round, since an MA(q) only depends directly on the last q errors, so the ACF cuts off and the PACF decays. To pick an AR model, the ACF decay and the PACF spike have to line up, and for an MA model it is the opposite. The lecture made it clear the table is a guide and not a hard rule, because sample ACFs are noisy, so the final choice also uses information criteria and residual diagnostics.

**From ARMA to ARIMA.** Many real series show both patterns at once, which is what ARMA is for, as it combines the AR and MA parts into one model. An ARMA process has both the ACF and PACF decaying, so you cannot pick its order from the plots alone and need AIC or BIC and the diagnostics as well.

ARIMA then adds differencing to ARMA so it can handle a series that is not stationary. The order $d$ is the number of times the series is differenced before the ARMA(p, q) part is fitted:

$$\phi(L)(1-L)^d y_t = c + \theta(L)\varepsilon_t$$

The result is the removal of the trend. For a series with a straight line trend, one difference leaves a constant plus noise, and for a random walk one difference leaves white noise. So ARIMA is ARMA with a differencing step first, which makes the series stationary before the AR and MA parts are fitted.

**What I want to keep in mind.** It is easy to keep differencing to get stationarity, but the notes show you can tell when you have gone too far. An over-differenced series has a higher variance than before and a lag 1 autocorrelation close to -0.5. So if differencing makes the variance go up instead of down, it was one step too many.

**Link to Project 1.** These were the first actual time series models we learnt, and I was curious to see how they would be fitted to real data and not just the examples in the slides. This is where the idea for my first project came from, where I fitted AR, MA and ARIMA models to AAPL prices and returns.

**Takeaway:** this lecture was the first time the ACF and PACF became a tool for choosing a model and not just plots to look at. ARIMA also made more sense once I saw it as ARMA with a differencing step first, instead of a whole new model.
